chunks: What is the Fourier Transform?. The question: What is the Fourier Transform?
The Fourier Transform rewrites a signal. Instead of describing how it changes over time, it lists how much of each frequency the signal contains.
Any signal can be built by adding sine waves of different frequencies, sizes and shifts, and the transform tells you the recipe.
Nothing is lost, because you can add the sine waves back up to rebuild the signal. It is useful because a circuit treats each frequency separately.
Think of a chord on a piano. You hear one sound, but it is made of separate notes. The Fourier Transform is like a listener who names every note and how loud it is.
The spectrum is that list. One thing the chord picture hides is timing: each note also has a start position in its cycle, called phase, and the transform keeps that too.
The spectrum of a 1 milliseconds pulse is a sinc with nulls at 1 kilohertz, 2 kilohertz, 3 kilohertz, and so on. X(0) equals the pulse area. If you shorten the pulse to 0.
1 milliseconds, the first null moves out to 10 kilohertz: shorter in time means wider in frequency. Drag T down to 0.
25 milliseconds: the first null moves out to 4 kilohertz while the peak (the area) falls to a quarter, so narrow in time means wide in frequency.
Frequency: how many cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Sine wave: a smooth, repeating wave at a single frequency.
Spectrum: the list of how much of each frequency is present. Phase: where in its cycle a sine wave starts. Rise time: how long a signal takes to go from low to high.
FFT: a fast way to compute the transform from sampled data. for sampling.
Take a rectangular pulse 1 milliseconds wide. Its spectrum drops to zero first at 1 ÷ 1 milliseconds = 1 kilohertz. Shorten the pulse to 0.
25 milliseconds and the first zero moves out to 4 kilohertz. So a shorter pulse spreads over more frequencies.
The same idea gives the edge rule: bandwidth (the range of frequencies that matter) is about 0. 35 ÷ rise time.
A 1 nanoseconds edge has meaningful content out to about 350 megahertz, even if the signal repeats far more slowly. That is the whole idea.
